Base directory for this skill: /home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/skills/plan-review-cycle

# Plan Review Cycle

Radice del plugin: `/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0`. Nei file di questa skill che leggi con Read, `/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0` vale questo percorso: sostituiscilo prima di eseguire un comando.

Prima di ogni comando Bash o PowerShell, scrivi `description` secondo `/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/docs/descrizione-comandi.md`.

You orchestrate a bounded planning and adversarial review workflow: a plan inside the spec file, reviewed by
the local `spec-plan-reviewer` agent until approved, a stop condition, or the budget. Do not implement code.
Where the rest lives — read a file only when this one sends you there:
- `autore.md` — how the plan is written and revised (plan shape, format 2, test level, floors): read by you at
  Step 1, and by the fresh author sub-agent of each format-2 revision;
- `revisori.md` — the reviewers' mandates: read by the reviewer agent itself;
- `formato-1.md` — a re-opened plan with no `Plan format: 2` line: read it only then;
- `plan-check.sh` — the code: structure, boundaries, differences, decisions (below). What moved out of this file
  into code, with its test: `/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/skills/full-implementation-cycle/riferimento.md`, «Rules in code».

.claude/.ai-workflow/spec-bytes-rounding-unit.md

## Single writable artifact

- You write only `.claude/.ai-workflow/spec-<name>.md`, and in it only `## Implementation plan` with its
  `### Plan review changelog`: never the spec sections above, never `## Implementation review`.
- The status lines (`Plan format: 2`, `Plan status:`, `Test level:`, `Risk surfaces:`, `Approved basis:`)
  are line-anchored and single-occurrence; prose and the changelog never reproduce those prefixes.
- **Languages (Maat 1.3.0)**: write the English headings and keywords (autore.md, «Languages»); every reader also
  accepts the Italian ones of older specs (`## Piano di implementazione`, `### Changelog revisione piano`,
  `Superfici a rischio:`…). A section that already exists keeps its heading: English only for a section created
  new, never both (`lint` VIOLAZIONE). An approved plan is never translated.
- **An approved plan is never edited**: only its changelog (notes, metric line). Any other change is a
  re-opening (below); `Approved basis:` makes a hand edit visible (`basis` → `STALE`, and the cycle stops).

## plan-check.sh — the code

`bash "/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/scripts/plan-check.sh" <cmd> …` — exit 0 ok · 1 `VIOLAZIONE` · 2 usage; an
`AVVISO` never changes the exit. A `VIOLAZIONE` is fixed before a reviewer sees the plan.
The keywords (`VIOLAZIONE`, `AVVISO`, `ERRORE DURO`, `Percorso:`, `Scheletro:`, `S2:`) are the same in every language;
the explanation after them follows `lingua` of `.claude/maat.json` (Maat 1.4.0).

| command | what it decides |
|---|---|
| `lint <spec> [--baseline <copy>]` | status lines, sections above untouched, surfaces and floors — before every round |
| `lint2 <spec>` | format 2: requirements ↔ tests ↔ steps ↔ files, blocks, test table and mutations, removed strings still asserted, Python test ids (`::`), reds that need a stub in an existing file; AVVISO for a module without `report` |
| `skeleton <spec>` | the size gate (skeleton and full plan); `Split: rejected` (or `Taglio: rifiutato`) in the spec → exit 0 |
| `split <mother> <child…>` | a cut: every requirement in exactly one child, `Depends on:` / `Interface for:` (or `Dipende da:` / `Interfaccia per:`) present |
| `route <spec>` | format 2 branch: `Percorso: leggero \| pieno — <motivo>` |
| `delta <copy> <spec>` | the `range:` lines rewritten since the copy, plus `xref:` lines; empty or whole-file → exit 1: that round runs at full scope |
| `s2 <spec> --delta <f> --gate <f> [--respinti <n>]` | `S2: APPROVA \| CORREGGI \| RILANCIA \| IMPRONTA DIVERSA \| STOP` |
| `basis <spec>` · `gen <spec>` | the fingerprint to record at approval · the downstream procedure (format 2) |

## `<name>`, container, re-opening

- A spec path → basename without `spec-`, normalised to `[a-z0-9._-]`. Pasted text → a kebab-case slug of its
  first heading (none → ask now) and the container, the text as `## Context` and `## Functional requirements`. No
  timestamps, no suffixes: an existing file is refined in place.
- **Re-opening an approved plan** (the only legal amendment): copy the spec to the scratchpad first (the delta
  baseline); new requirements are written above by the user or `spec-author`, never by you; `Plan status:
  DRAFT`, plus any missing status line (and a floor or `⚠️` line for a declared critical surface); the amendment
  as surgical edits, recorded in the changelog; then straight to the delta round, fresh budget. Format 1 →
  `formato-1.md`.

Run the whole cycle in one uninterrupted turn: no pause and no confirmation between steps, rounds, revisions.

## Budget and stops

**4 iterations** (format 2; format 1: `formato-1.md`): one fan-out, one S2 pair, one fresh-eyes run = one
iteration. At the budget without approval → `Plan status: NEEDS HUMAN DECISION`. Other stops, also →
`NEEDS HUMAN DECISION`: a `STOP_HUMAN_DECISION_REQUIRED` from any reviewer · a recurrence · a rejected finding
re-raised by the same producer with no new evidence (disagreement on a verifiable fact) · scope not in the spec
· an ambiguity the codebase cannot resolve · `skeleton` exit 1 (the cut proposal, Step 1).

## Findings

- Only `blocker`/`major` block, and only with a **verifiable anchor**: `code` (`path:line` that says it) ·
  `spec/plan` (a line contradicting or omitting something checkable) · `absence` (pattern + scope + 0 results) ·
  `measure` (a result of the declared remote verification you supplied). No anchor → optional.
- **Verify before applying**: 1 Read or 1 Grep on the anchor (real data: a read-only query of the remote verification, not under
  `--no-dev`). Reject **only if the anchor is literally false**, never on reasoning — you own the plan. A
  rejection: one changelog line `rifiutato: <key> — <refutation>`, the «Rejected» list of every later prompt and
  of the final response; it does not count toward recurrence.
- `minor`/`nit` are **never applied**, not even after approval: one changelog line each, notes for the
  implementer. A finding needed for correctness is a `major`.
- **One round, several reviewers**: a `STOP_HUMAN_DECISION_REQUIRED` dominates; one `NEEDS_CHANGES` makes the
  round `NEEDS_CHANGES`; `APPROVED` only if all approve.
- **A partial review is not an approval**: an `APPROVED` with `Blocked on:` or uncovered ranges → re-run that
  producer on those ranges, free once per producer and range; a second partial there costs an iteration, a
  third is `STOP_HUMAN_DECISION_REQUIRED`.
- **Recurrence is yours** (the reviewers are stateless): a table `key → state`, never the full reviews; key
  `<area>/<claim in 5 words>` plus its anchored symbol or path, never a line number; states `aperto · risolto ·
  rifiutato · reintrodotto`. The same blocker/major in two consecutive runs of the same producer →
  `STOP_HUMAN_DECISION_REQUIRED`; `reintrodotto` (a `risolto` key back after a later edit) is a label, not a stop.

## Step 1: the plan

Level: `--tests=min|std|full` (aliases «test minimi», «solo i gate» → `min`; «test completi», «tutti i test» →
`full`), default `std`. You write the plan yourself: read `/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/skills/plan-review-cycle/autore.md` now and
follow it. Copy the spec to the scratchpad (the `lint` baseline), write the **skeleton** only, then `skeleton`:
- `SOTTO IL TETTO` → write the full plan from the skeleton; then `lint --baseline`,
  `lint2`, `skeleton` again (the full-plan ceiling), `route`, and refresh the context pack
  (`bash "/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/scripts/context-pack.sh" <spec>`: the plan changed the spec's fingerprint);
- `SOPRA IL TETTO` → **cut proposal**: `maat:spec-author` in mode `split` (Task) with the spec path and the `skeleton`
  output; `split <spec> <children…>`; a `VIOLAZIONE` goes back to `maat:spec-author` once, again → report it. Then
  `Plan status: NEEDS HUMAN DECISION`, changelog note «scheletro sopra il tetto: proposta di taglio in N
  anelli», and stop with the proposal: the rings in order, their requirements, what users see between rings.
  The user decides once; a rejection is recorded above the plan by `spec-author` (`Split: rejected —
  <date>`; `Taglio: rifiutato` in an older spec), and from then on `skeleton` lets the single plan go on.

**Branch.** `--full` always wins. Otherwise `route`: `Percorso: leggero` → the rounds of
`plan-review-cycle-light`; `pieno` → Step 2 (`--light` is honoured only with `leggero`). Say it in one line.

## Step 2: round 1 — three lenses in one message

Three `maat:spec-plan-reviewer` agents in a single message, each: «Use the maat:spec-plan-reviewer agent. Read
`/home/bench/bench-run-config/plugins/cache/maat/maat/1.6.0/skills/plan-review-cycle/revisori.md`, section «Round 1», and follow it. Lens: <L1|L2|L3>. Spec + plan
file: <path>. Ranges: spec <offset/limit>, plan <offset/limit>. Context pack: <path | none>. Test level: <lvl>.
Risk surfaces: <tokens>.» Aggregate. `APPROVED` outright → Step 3, but first one fresh-eyes reviewer
alone when a critical surface (`permissions`, `data`, `destructive` — `permessi`, `dati`, `distruttiva`) is declared.

## S2: revise, then delta ∥ fresh eyes (every later round)

1. Verify each blocker/major. Copy the spec to the scratchpad, then — **the author is fresh at every round**, you
   keep the finding table and the recurrence — an author sub-agent (Task): the spec path, the
   findings to apply with their verified anchors, «read `autore.md`, section «How to revise», apply only these».
   Then `lint --baseline`, `lint2`, `delta <copy> <spec>`. All findings rejected → no author, no delta: step 2.
2. One message, two `maat:spec-plan-reviewer` agents on the same plan — «read `revisori.md`, section «Delta»» and
   «… section «Fresh eyes»» — with: the `range:` and `xref:` lines, the pertinent requirement ranges, level and
   surfaces (every round), resolved findings (key + symbol + one line), rejected ones (key + refutation), test
   cases removed as over-testing, budget ~20 → 15 → 12. Save each reply to the scratchpad with, as first line,
   `Impronta piano: <plan value of basis at launch>`.
3. `s2 <spec> --delta <f> --gate <f> --respinti <n>` (`n` = the blocker/major of **these two** replies you
   rejected): `APPROVA` → Step 3 · `CORREGGI` → next round · `RILANCIA` → both again, together, with the
   rejected list · `IMPRONTA DIVERSA` → relaunch on the current plan · `STOP` → `NEEDS HUMAN DECISION`.

## Step 3: decide

- **Approved** → `Plan status: APPROVED`; `basis <spec>` and its whole `Basis:` value as `Approved basis: <value>`
  right under `Risk surfaces:` (or `Superfici a rischio:`) (replacing an older one; a ring's `madre`/`prec`/`interfaccia` included);
  `basis` again must say `FRESH`; format 2: `gen <spec>` must exit 0. Never write ` · tests <fp>`: the test-red
  phase does. Then, in the changelog only, the optional findings as notes and the metric line.
- **Not approved** (budget, stop) → `Plan status: NEEDS HUMAN DECISION`, the open decision, the metric line.

The **metric line**, last line of the changelog (no backticks, never the status prefixes; one per run of the
cycle): `Metrica ciclo: giri=5 · R1=2/3 · delta=1/2 · gate=0/1 · rifiutati=1 · ricorrenze=0 · reintrodotti=1 ·
esito=approvato · livello=std · superfici=permessi,dati · formato=2` (`R1`/`delta`/`gate` = blocker/major found
in that phase over its runs; `giri` = iterations).

## Final response

`Decision:` · the spec file · `Plan status:` · summary · unresolved blocker/major · rejected findings (key +
refutation) · optional findings, not applied · `Test level: <lvl> (<default std | esplicito | alias>)` ·
`Risk surfaces:` with the floor of each critical surface (or its `⚠️`) · next command: approved →
`/maat:implementation-review-cycle <name>`, saying plainly that **plan approval does not replace the code review**
(the quick `--light` round after implementing is always worth it); not approved → the human decision needed. A
`/browser-qa` suggestion only when the plan changes a multi-step UI journey or wires UI state to persistence with
no component test — for the human, never in the plan.

182	func logn(n, b float64) float64 {
183		return math.Log(n) / math.Log(b)
184	}
185	
186	func countDigits(n int64) int {
187		digits := 0
188		for n != 0 {
189			n /= 10
190			digits += 1
191		}
192		return digits
193	}
194	
195	func humanateBytes(s uint64, base float64, minDigits int, sizes []string) string {
196		if s < 10 {
197			return fmt.Sprintf("%d B", s)
198		}
199		e := math.Floor(logn(float64(s), base))
200		suffix := sizes[int(e)]
201		val := float64(s) / math.Pow(base, e)
202	
203		// Determine how many decimal places to keep based on the unrounded
204		// value's integer-digit count, then round exactly once to that
205		// precision. Rounding first to a fixed precision and then again when
206		// formatting (double rounding) can flip the result at a boundary due
207		// to floating point error (see #103).
208		intDigits := countDigits(int64(val))
209		digits := max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
210		rounding := math.Pow10(digits)
211		val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding
212	
213		// Rounding may have carried into an additional integer digit (e.g.
214		// 9.996 -> 10.0), which means fewer decimal places should be shown
215		// than originally computed.
216		if newIntDigits := countDigits(int64(val)); newIntDigits > intDigits {
217			digits = max(digits-(newIntDigits-intDigits), 0)
218		}
219	
220		ff := "%%.%df %%s"
221		f := fmt.Sprintf(ff, digits)
222		return fmt.Sprintf(f, val, suffix)
223	}

272	// ParseBytes parses a string representation of bytes into the number
273	// of bytes it represents.
274	//
275	// See Also: Bytes, IBytes.
276	//
277	// ParseBytes("42 MB") -> 42000000, nil
278	// ParseBytes("42 mib") -> 44040192, nil
279	func ParseBytes(s string) (uint64, error) {
280		lastDigit := 0
281		hasComma := false
282		for _, r := range s {
283			if !(unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '.' || r == ',') {
284				break
285			}
286			if r == ',' {
287				hasComma = true
288			}
289			lastDigit++
290		}
291	
292		num := s[:lastDigit]
293		if hasComma {
294			num = strings.Replace(num, ",", "", -1)
295		}
296	
297		f, err := strconv.ParseFloat(num, 64)
298		if err != nil {
299			return 0, err
300		}
301	
302		extra := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s[lastDigit:]))
303		if m, ok := bytesSizeTable[extra]; ok {
304			// Parse whole-number inputs exactly. A float64 cannot represent
305			// integers above 2^53, and the multiplication below would also reject
306			// otherwise-valid values near math.MaxUint64, so route integers through
307			// uint64 arithmetic with an overflow check.
308			if !strings.ContainsRune(num, '.') {
309				if v, perr := strconv.ParseUint(num, 10, 64); perr == nil {
310					if hi, lo := bits.Mul64(v, m); hi == 0 {
311						return lo, nil
312					}
313					return 0, fmt.Errorf("too large: %v", s)
314				}
315			}
316			f *= float64(m)
317			if f >= math.MaxUint64 {
318				return 0, fmt.Errorf("too large: %v", s)
319			}
320			return uint64(f), nil
321		}
322	
323		return 0, fmt.Errorf("unhandled size name: %v", extra)
324	}

526	No other files are created or modified (no `plan-<name>.md`, no `spec.md`, no versioned

552	`## Piano di implementazione`, `### Piano di test`, `Superfici a rischio:`, `[pavimento:`, `rosso se:`…) and never

583	## Risk surfaces
584	
585	**The risk-surface vocabulary — the single list; every other mention points here:**
586	
587	| Token | Italian token (older plans) | Covers | Critical |
588	|---|---|---|---|
589	| `permissions` | `permessi` | authentication, authorization, roles, visibility by role | **yes** |
590	| `data` | `dati` | DB schema, migrations, persistent state, data written or deleted in bulk | **yes** |
591	| `destructive` | `distruttiva` | an operation that deletes or overwrites data/state irreversibly | **yes** |
592	| `api-contract` | `contratto-api` | request/response shape, status codes, routes consumed by others | no |
593	| `import` | `import` | the import pipelines | no |
594	| `shared-logic` | `logica-condivisa` | shared business logic, shared components/stores/composables | no |
595	
596	The plan declares the touched ones in `Risk surfaces:` — bare tokens separated by commas,
597	or `none`; no notes on that line (`plan-check.sh lint` rejects an unknown token). The two columns are the same
598	token: `plan-check.sh` maps the English one to the Italian one, and prints the Italian one (`Pavimento: permessi`). **Critical** surfaces drive two things and nothing else: the verification floor
599	(see "Test effort") and the fresh-eyes gate after a round-1 approval (Step 2-ter). No
600	LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH grading: no behaviour needs it. Lens L1 verifies the declaration like any
601	`no implication` — under-declaring would silently skip both.
602	
603	## Test effort: `--tests=min|std|full`
604	
605	Parse `$ARGUMENTS` for `--tests=min|std|full`. Italian aliases count as the flag: "test minimi" /
606	"solo i gate" → `min`; "test completi" / "tutti i test" → `full`. **Default: `std`.**
607	
608	Write the resolved level into the plan as `Test level: <lvl>`, immediately under `Plan status:`
609	(single occurrence, line-anchored — see the hard rules above). This line is how
610	`/implementation-review-cycle` learns the level; it is the only channel.
611	
612	| | `min` | `std` (default) | `full` |
613	|---|---|---|---|
614	| Suite | existing gates of the **touched modules only** | same | modules' suites + lint (the CI's gates; build only if the plan prescribes it) |
615	| New test cases in the plan | **0**, unless a bug regression (1 case) | **≤5**, only on the behavior the plan changes | no cap |
616	| `[floor:` line per declared critical surface | 1, outside the caps | 1, outside the caps | 1, outside the caps |
617	| Counterproof (the file(s) it names reverted to base, or a named mutation; expected red) | none | on the **central gate** only (1, max 2) | every new case |
618	| e2e prescribed in the plan | only `[e2e-locator:` (below) | only `[e2e-locator:` (below) | at most 1 targeted spec, plus `[e2e-locator:` |
619	| `/browser-qa` | never | never | **never** — explicit request only |
620	| Length of `### Test plan` (a signal, never a finding by itself) | ~1 line | ~15 lines | free |
621	
622	**A whole-suite gate is permitted but never required at `full`; it is forbidden at `min` and
623	`std`.** This is the criterion L3 uses to decide whether a gate is over-testing, so it must be
624	unambiguous.
625	
626	**Section name.** The canonical heading is `### Test plan` (numbering optional, e.g.
627	`### 9. Test plan`; `### Piano di test` in an older plan, kept as it is). The length rule targets this heading.
628	Plan headings and keywords are written in English as shown here (`### Requirement traceability`, `red if:`…),
629	whatever the language of the prose — see «Languages» above for the sections that already exist.
630	
631	**The length is measured, not enforced.** `plan-check.sh lint` prints an `AVVISO` above it; a
632	reviewer never raises a blocker/major on the line count alone — what blocks is what the lines
633	prescribe (a case over the level's cap, a duplicate, a whole suite below `full`). Measured: a major
634	"over the 15-line cap" cost a round and was resolved by merging lines, not by removing a test.
635	
636	**Risk surfaces do NOT raise the level — but a critical one gets a floor.** The level is the
637	verification *budget*; it never turns `min` into `full`. Yet at `min` a permission change could
638	otherwise reach approval with no verification of the permission at all. So, for **each critical
639	surface declared** (`permissions`, `data`, `destructive` — vocabulary in «Risk surfaces»), `### Test plan`
640	names **exactly one** pertinent verification, as a list item of its own, marked:
641	
642	```text
643	- [floor: permissions] <an existing test cited by path, OR 1 new case, OR a read-only DB check of the declared remote verification> red if: <condition>
644	```
645	
646	- for `permissions`, the pertinent verification is the **negative** one (the denied role is denied);
647	- a `[floor:` line (`[pavimento:` in an older plan) is **exempt** from the level's caps (new cases, `### Test plan` length),
648	  from the L3 over-testing rule and from the "do NOT re-add" list — at most one per critical
649	  surface, which `plan-check.sh lint` enforces;
650	- if no pertinent verification is reachable, the plan writes the old **one line** instead —
651	  `⚠️ Surface <token> not covered by the gates at level <lvl>`, with the vocabulary token right
652	  after `Surface` (a `⚠️` line about another surface does not cover this one) — and continues.
653	  One line, not a paragraph, and outside the caps too. **Downstream it is an obligation**: the
654	  feature cannot reach `IMPLEMENTED` until the user reports a verification of that surface — i.e.
655	  in `/full-implementation-cycle` a `⚠️` on a critical surface **is a human STOP**. That is the
656	  honest reading of "no gate can cover it"; before, it came out `VERIFIED` with nothing having
657	  touched the surface at runtime. So look hard for a floor first;
658	- **the waiver**: when the change does not alter the surface's runtime behaviour at all (a rename,
659	  a message, a refactor that leaves the check itself untouched), append on the **same physical
660	  line** `— static sufficient: <reason>`. Then no obligation arises downstream; the surface stays
661	  a risk focus. L3 judges the motive: a waiver on a change that does alter the behaviour is
662	  under-testing. After approval the line is frozen (`Approved basis:`);
663	- non-critical surfaces (`api-contract`, `shared-logic`, `import`) get no floor and no
664	  obligation: their risk is blast radius, which is L1/L2's job, not a test's. A `⚠️` line on them
665	  is only a risk focus.
666	
667	**Every new test case states `red if: <condition>`** — the world in which it goes red. One
668	clause per case, no new cap: it makes L3's non-vacuity check checkable instead of inferred.
669	
670	**A counterproof names the file(s) it touches** — either reverted to the base, or a **named
671	mutation** (file · symbol · what is removed, e.g. "remove the `!= ROLE_MANAGER` condition in
672	`resolve_membership()`") — then the expected red. Use the mutation when the test imports something
673	the feature adds: a file back at base then fails on the import, not on the assertion (measured,
674	`spec-golas-obiettivo-aziendale`: an ImportError, a FAIL, a round and a human decision). Never
675	"revert the whole feature" nor a `git stash`: `/full-implementation-cycle` touches only the files a
676	gate names and records a gate that names none as `NOT RUN` — a STOP.
677	
678	**An e2e bound to a locator, at any level.** When the plan changes a file in `e2e/specs/`, or a
679	string, class or attribute that an e2e spec uses as a locator (L3 searches every changed string
680	there), `### Test plan` carries one list item per affected spec:
681	
682	```text
683	- [e2e-locator: e2e-6-customer.spec.ts] <the locator or string that changes> red if: <condition>
684	```
685	
686	At most 2 such lines; beyond that, one `⚠️` line and the regression watch. They are outside the
687	level's caps like a `[floor:` line (`plan-check.sh lint` does not count them, the
688	`Approved basis:`
689	fingerprint freezes them), and downstream each is a required gate: the declared remote verification (`verifica_remota` in `.claude/maat.json`) with `--e2e <spec>` on DEV, so with
690	`--no-dev` the feature stops at `NEEDS_VERIFICATION` — on purpose. Measured: unit tests green while the real DOM broke a locator (`spec-partita-iva-unica-context`), and a selector changed at `std` whose e2e never ran (`spec-opzioni-offerta-salvataggio`).
691	
692	**`/browser-qa` is never prescribed in a plan**, at any level: it is a separate flow, invoked by
693	hand when needed (and it stays a mandatory gate only at the porting cutover).
694	
695	**Downstream contract — these lines are consumed, not just read.** `/implementation-review-cycle`
696	parses the approved plan with `plan-check.sh contract` and does NOT re-derive what the plan already
697	decided:
698	- every gate written in `### Test plan` becomes a **required gate** of the implementation
699	  review (a feature cannot reach `IMPLEMENTED` until it has passed on the reviewed code). So write
700	  each gate as something that can be executed and observed — a test file, a command, a counterproof
701	  with its expected red — never as a wish ("verify that it works");
702	- every `⚠️ Surface <token> not covered…` line becomes a **risk focus** the implementation reviewer
703	  must look at first: keep it to the surfaces that are really uncovered;
704	- the surfaces of `Risk surfaces:` are a risk focus too, a `[floor:` or `[e2e-locator:`
705	  line is a required gate like any other, a critical surface with neither a floor nor a waiver is an
706	  **obligation** closed only by the user's evidence, and `### Requirement traceability` is the
707	  requirement list the implementation reviewer reports coverage against.
708	Over-prescribing here therefore costs twice: once in the plan, once as a gate that must pass.

711

713	above `Plan status:`, line-anchored, single occurrence — is in **format 2**. **Every plan this skill
714	writes from scratch is in format 2.** A plan without the line is **format 1** and follows the rest of
715	this file exactly as before — a format-1 plan re-opened later included: it is never converted.
716	Everything above (status lines, level, surfaces, floors, `red if:`, `Approved basis:`) holds in both.

718	**Structure.** H3 sections (numbering optional); the table headers are fixed — `plan-check.sh` reads

733	
734	### Touched files
735	- `backend/app/routers/goals.py`
736	- `backend/tests/test_goals.py`
737	
738	### Steps
739	#### Block B1 — backend
740	writes: `backend/app/routers/goals.py`, `backend/tests/test_goals.py`
741	after: none
742	
743	| id | file | change | test |
744	|---|---|---|---|
745	| P1 | `backend/app/routers/goals.py` | `update_goal()`: 403 for whoever cannot edit | T1 |
746

762	
763	### Test plan

765	|---|---|---|---|---|
766	| T1 | FR1 | `backend/tests/test_goals.py::test_update_denied` (new) | red if: a salesperson updates the target | `backend/app/routers/goals.py` · `update_goal` · `if not can_edit:` → `if False:` · red if: `assert 200 == 403` |

770	The Italian forms of an older format-2 plan, kept where the section already exists: `## Piano di implementazione`,
771	`### Decisioni` · `### File toccati` · `### Passi` · `### Tracciabilità requisiti` · `### Stringhe e data-test` ·
772	`### Piano di test`, `#### Blocco <id>` with `scrive:` / `dopo:` (`nessuno`), the headers `id | file | modifica |
773	test`, `azione | tipo | valore` (`aggiunge` / `toglie`, `stringa` / `data-test`, column `verificato`),
774	`ID | requisito | file | asserzione | mutazione`, `rosso se:`, `(vuoto)`, `(nuovo)`, `[pavimento: <token>]`,
775	`⚠️ Rischio aperto`. Each reader accepts both.
776	
777	- **Paths** are relative to the repository, everywhere (their first segment exists at the root).
778	- **New files**: in `### Touched files`, `(new)` right after the path's code span (`` - `path` (new) ``)
779	  marks a file the plan creates. Downstream (harness-pt11) it is the `test-red` phase's write scope with the
780	  test files, where the stubs of the new symbols go, and the only kind of file whose counterproof can be
781	  absorbed (L2).
782	- **Acceptance tests (test-red)**: every row of `### Test plan` is written and proven red on the base with
783	  stubs before the implementation. The red must hit the row's assertion, at a position in the test file: put
784	  the expected failure text between backticks in `assertion` (else the mutation's `red if:` is used) — a row
785	  with neither is a `lint2` VIOLATION, and a red with no text or no position is not proven; every string or `data-test` the plan
786	  adds must be listed as `adds` in `### Strings and data-test` — an existing test asserting its absence is
787	  a conflict that stops the phase.
788	- **Stubs go only into new files.** A new parameter (or an extra positional argument) of a function that already
789	  exists gets no signature stub: on the base the test fails with the `TypeError` of the call, before its assertion.
790	  Its red is that one — `` red if: `unexpected keyword argument 'sep'` `` (or `` `positional argument` ``) — not the
791	  value the implementation will return; the mutation's `red if:` keeps the value (it runs on the implemented code).
792	  `lint2` gives a VIOLATION when a Python call in the row's backticks does not fit the signature of an existing
793	  function of `### Touched files` and the row's red does not name the `TypeError`.
794	- **Reports.** The test-red phase reads the outcome of each test from the module's report (`report: junit` or
795	  `vitest` in `.claude/maat.json`): a row in a module with `report: nessuno` gets a `lint2` AVVISO, because the phase
796	  would stop BLOCKED. It is configuration, not plan: say it to the user in the round's summary, do not rewrite the plan
797	  for it.
798	- **Decisions** stay prose; the input → output examples are what the implementer and the tests read.
799	- **Steps**: every step is a row `id | file | change | test` inside a `#### Block <id>`; each block
800	  declares `writes:` (the files it writes) and `after:` (the blocks it depends on, or `none`).
801	- **Test plan**: one row per case. `file` = the test, as the first code span: `path` or
802	  `path::name` (pytest node id, or vitest full name — required when the row has a mutation; a Python class and
803	  its method are separated by `::` even for `unittest` tests: `test_x.py::TestX::test_y`, never `TestX.test_y`,
804	  a `lint2` VIOLATION; a pytest doctest id keeps its dots: `mod.py::mod.func`); `(new)`
805	  after the span marks a new case, the one the level's caps count. `assertion` = the case's
806	  `red if:`. `requirement` = the IDs of `### Requirement traceability` it verifies.
807	- **Existing non-regression tests are NOT rows of `### Test plan`.** A test that already exists and must
808	  only stay green («stays green», «remains green», «keeps passing» — or the Italian «resta verde», «rimane verde»,
809	  «continua a passare») cannot be proven red on the base with stubs, so as a row it stops the cycle at test-red —
810	  `lint2` gives a VIOLATION for a row whose `assertion` starts that way. Put them in a note right under the table,
811	  one item each: «EXISTING non-regression tests (not rows of the Test plan: they cannot be proven red on the base
812	  with stubs):» — `path` (or `path::name`), what stays true, the requirement IDs, and the explicit command when the
813	  test is outside the gate of the touched modules. A requirement covered only by such a test is written in
814	  `### Requirement traceability` as ``not verifiable by a test (invariance, cannot be proven red): covered by the
815	  existing test `<path>` `` (the `not verifiable` prefix — or `non verificabile` — is what `lint2` accepts); the
816	  step's `test` column then names no ID for it (`—`). A test the plan **updates** is not «stays green»: it is a row
817	  with its `red if:`.
818	- **mutation** = the counterproof, in `counterproof.sh`'s form, or `—`:
819	  `` `file` · `symbol` · `search` → `replace` · red if: `text of the error message` ``.
820	  `(empty)` in place of the replacement removes `search`; `search` must occur **once** in the file
821	  *after* the implementation; a `|` is written `\|`, a backtick needs a double-backtick span. File and
822	  test in the same module of `.claude/maat.json` (a test under the `radice` of the file's module). Which rows
823	  carry one follows the level (none at `min`, the central gate at `std`, every new case at `full`).
824	- `[floor:`, `[e2e-locator:` and `⚠️` lines stay list items under the table, as in format 1; a
825	  floor that is a row of the table names its ID.
826	- **Strings and data-test**: every string or `data-test` the plan removes (`removes`) or adds (`adds`).
827	  `lint2` searches the existing tests for them and decides, by the literal's position, whether a match asserts
828	  presence (a `VIOLAZIONE` unless the file is one the plan touches — an e2e spec: its `[e2e-locator:` line) or
829	  absence (an `AVVISO`). An optional fourth column `verified` — `` `<file>` — <reason> `` — waives that row's
830	  match in that file: `| removes | string | `Active` | `frontend/tests/x.test.ts` — rewritten by flow X |`.
831	- **A product defect found late** (round 3 or 4) does not reopen the design: it becomes one test row, with its
832	  step, and one list item `⚠️ Open risk: <claim> — <test ID>` under the table.
833	
834	**Generated, never written.** The plan carries **no** command line, no `test-fast.sh` path list, no
835	pytest selector, no counterproof recipe: `plan-check.sh gen <spec>` derives them from the test table and
836	writes them to the run directory — `<spec>.run/gen/procedura.txt` (level, commands, paths, blocks) and
837	`<spec>.run/counterproof/mutations.json` (the list `counterproof.sh` reads; removed when no row has a
838	mutation). A procedure written by hand cannot be wrong, because there is none.

841	
842	A plan too large does not converge (the reviewers sample it instead of exhausting it). Asked for the skeleton:
843	1. **Skeleton first.** Write only the skeleton into the plan section: `Plan format: 2` and the status lines
844	   (`Plan status: DRAFT`), `### Touched files`, and `### Steps` with its `#### Block` blocks and one row per
845	   step (`| id | file | change | test |` — a few words in `change`, `test` may be `—`). No decisions, no
846	   traceability, no test plan yet. Then `plan-check.sh skeleton <spec>`:
847	   - `Scheletro: SOTTO IL TETTO` (≤15 steps, ≤40 files) → write the full plan **starting from the skeleton**
848	     (it is its backbone: nothing is thrown away);
849	   - `Scheletro: SOPRA IL TETTO` (exit 1) → **cut proposal** (below).
850	   The orchestrator runs `plan-check.sh skeleton` (ceilings in its constants: ≤15 steps, ≤40 files, a full plan
851	   ≤400 lines) and, under them, asks for the full plan **starting from the skeleton** (nothing is thrown away).

853	## Writing the plan
854	
855	Analyze the local codebase and write the `## Implementation plan` section into
856	`.claude/.ai-workflow/spec-<name>.md` with `Plan status: DRAFT`, `Test level: <lvl>` and
857	`Risk surfaces: <tokens | none>`. Copy the spec to the scratchpad **before** writing
858	(the `lint` baseline), and after writing run `plan-check.sh lint <spec> --baseline <copy>`.
859	
860	**`### Requirement traceability`** — one row per requirement, with the ID as the spec writes it
861	(`FR1`, `RF1` in an older spec, `D3`, `Requirement A`…) or `FR<n>` by position when the spec has none. Cite the
862	spec's ids literally: `RF1` and `FR1` are **different** ids (no alias), and a chain ring uses its mother's family:
863	
864	```text
865	| Req | Plan steps | Verification |
866	| FR1 | 2, 3 | test_x.py::test_y · or: not verifiable by a test, <reason> |
867	```
868	
869	One row each, no prose: a small feature gets a three-row table. L1 checks it (not a script: real
870	specs number requirements in too many ways for a count to be reliable).
871	
872	The plan must cover: objective; relevant files/components/stores/services/routes/tests/
873	APIs; current behavior; proposed behavior; implementation steps; data-flow implications;
874	UI implications; backend implications; validation rules; permission rules; migration/
875	persistence implications; risks; requirement traceability (below); test plan **at the declared
876	level** (see "Test effort"); rollback considerations; explicit out-of-scope.
877	
878	**Size the plan to the change — these sections are conditional, not mandatory prose.**
879	A section with nothing to say gets **one line, `no implication`** — never a paragraph of
880	filler. Measured: plans average ~700 lines and reach 1314, and that volume is the surface every
881	round rewrites, which is where self-inflicted defects come from. An explicit `no
882	implication` is a verifiable claim; filler prose is indistinguishable from real content, to a
883	human reader and to a reviewer alike.
884	
885	Lens **L1** is required to check every one of those declarations, so writing one without
886	looking will be caught.
887	
888	**Three constraints on the test plan**, on top of the level's caps:
889	
890	- **suite selection follows the diff**: FE-only change → no `pytest`; BE-only → no `vitest`. Derive
891	  the selectors the way the module's `regola_test` in `.claude/maat.json` maps sources to tests
892	  (`maat-config.py test-di`); do not reinvent it;
893	- **no whole-suite gate** at `min`/`std`: the gate is the touched modules' suite;
894	- **never prescribe `/browser-qa`** — separate flow, invoked by hand.
895	
896	Do not write code. Do not modify source files. Do not touch the spec sections above.
897	
898	**Context pack first.** If `.claude/.ai-workflow/spec-<name>.run/context-pack.md` exists (the full cycle
899	generates it; by hand: `bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/context-pack.sh" .claude/.ai-workflow/spec-<name>.md`), read it
900	**before** exploring the code: the files the spec names (verified: they exist or not), their signatures,
901	the tests that cite them, the DB columns. It is orientation, not authority — **the code wins over the
902	pack**: code reads stay allowed, and whatever the plan cites (`path:line`, a name, a count) is still
903	checked in the code. After writing the plan, and before launching the lenses, re-run the same command:
904	the plan changed the spec's fingerprint, so the pack is regenerated with the plan's files too (unchanged
905	spec → it writes nothing). A missing pack or a failed run changes nothing: explore as before.
906	
907	**Reading, in this step and in every revision.**
908	- *Targeted first.* Start from a search (Grep/Glob) and read the ranges it points to; widen a range,
909	  or read a file whole, only when those ranges do not settle the question (a short file may be read
910	  whole). This narrows how you read, not what you check: every file, consumer and surface the plan
911	  needs is still read.
912	- *No stale re-reads, no stale quotes.* Do not re-read a range already in your context and unchanged
913	  since; do not `cat`/`sed -n` a file you are about to Read. A range becomes stale — re-read it —
914	  after: an Edit/Write of yours, or a `cp`/`mv`/redirection, on that file (that file only; so is
915	  `review-surface.sh diff --out <file>`); a sub-agent that can write, a test, build, formatter,
916	  generator or any other Bash command (everything — and everything stays stale while such a task runs
917	  in background); a compaction or a change of phase (everything). Read/Grep/Glob, a sub-agent whose
918	  `tools:` are only Read/Grep/Glob (the reviewers — by the frontmatter, not by the name), read-only
919	  commands (`grep`, `ls`, `wc`, `git status|log|diff|show` without redirections), `plan-check.sh`
920	  and `review-surface.sh snapshot|check|test-signals` stale nothing. When in doubt, everything is
921	  stale. Whatever you quote — an Edit `old_string`, a gate, a finding, a `path:line` — comes from a
922	  read still valid under these rules, never from memory.
923	- *Batch only what is independent*: calls that do not depend on each other's results go in one
924	  message; never two Edits on the same file, nor a write with what must see it. Batching changes only
925	  how the same necessary operations travel: never fewer searches, reads or checks to save turns.
926	- The reviewers still read everything they need from scratch: this rule is about your own repeated
927	  reads, not theirs.
928	
929	**Optional dynamic check of DB assumptions (remote verification).** First, parse `$ARGUMENTS`: if it contains
930	`--no-dev` (or "review veloce" / "senza DEV"), skip this check entirely. Otherwise, when the plan
931	asserts facts about real data/schema (a column is nullable, an enum's values, a row's
932	existence/cardinality), verify them with a read-only query of the declared remote verification (`verifica_remota` in `.claude/maat.json`) instead of
933	deducing them statically, and feed the result into the plan/review. This runs ONLY when the plan makes
934	such a DB assertion (no assertion → nothing to run, no DEV roundtrip). `spec-plan-reviewer` stays a
935	static `Read/Grep/Glob` agent — it does NOT get Bash; the verification is this separate step.
936	
937	### How to revise: surgically, never by rewriting
938	
939	Apply each blocking finding as **one minimal, localized Edit**. Do not rewrite the section, do
940	not reorganize "while you are in there", and **do not touch a code block inside the plan unless
941	the finding is about that block**. This is the single rule that attacks the round multiplier
942	head-on: nine specs record that their late-round blockers were introduced by the previous
943	round's own revision. If a finding genuinely requires restructuring, do it — and flag that block
944	so the next round reviews it in full.
945	
946	**Measure every list you write.** Any list or count of `file:line`, occurrences or consumers that a
947	revision writes comes from a search run **just before** writing it — never from memory or from
948	the finding's text. Measured on `spec-restyling-ui-soft`: 3 of the 4 blockers raised against
949	revisions were lists of points written by inference, and "the total still adds up" hid the error
950	each time.

# Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit

## Context

The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
that should have been written with the next unit:

- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.

The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).

## Goal

No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.

## Functional requirements

FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.

FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.

FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.

FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.

FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
that is promoted and the largest one that is not).

FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.

## Codebase areas involved (indicative)

- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.

## Acceptance criteria

AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.

AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.

AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.

AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.

## Assumptions

- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
  `%.1f` formatting.

## Out of scope

- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
- New dependencies.

## Constraints

- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
- `gofmt` formatting.

### Decisions
**D1 — `IBytesN` keeps its current output.** `humanateBytes` also serves `IBytesN` (`bytes.go:150-153`), which the spec never names. FR1 lists five functions, FR5, FR6 and AC4 say five, and FR2 says every other output is unchanged, so `IBytesN` is not promoted, even though the Goal's wording («no byte formatter») would reach it. The requirements are the checkable text and this is the narrower reading: extending it later is one changed argument (`false` → `true`). The helper therefore gets an explicit parameter `promote bool`: `true` from `Bytes`, `BytesN`, `IBytes`; `false` from `IBytesN`. `humanateBytes` has no other caller (`bytes.go:115,128,138,152`) and no test calls it directly.

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `IBytesN(1_048_575, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
| `IBytesN(1_048_064, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
| `IBytesN(1_048_063, 2)` | `1023 KiB` (unchanged) |

**D2 — `humanateBytes`: promote after the rounding, without recursion.** Right after `val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding` and before the carry adjustment of `digits`:

```go
if promote && val >= base && int(e)+1 < len(sizes) {
	suffix = sizes[int(e)+1]
	val, intDigits = 1, 1
	digits = max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
}

# Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit

## Context

The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
that should have been written with the next unit:

- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.

The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).

## Goal

No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.

## Functional requirements

FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.

FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.

FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.

FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.

FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
that is promoted and the largest one that is not).

FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.

## Codebase areas involved (indicative)

- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.

## Acceptance criteria

AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.

AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.

AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.

AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.

## Assumptions

- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
  `%.1f` formatting.

## Out of scope

- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
- New dependencies.

## Constraints

- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
- `gofmt` formatting.

Above 2^53 `float64(s)` loses precision, so the two highest boundaries of `Bytes` and `IBytes` are not the exact half. # Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit

## Context

The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
that should have been written with the next unit:

- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.

The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).

## Goal

No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.

## Functional requirements

FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.

FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.

FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.

FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.

FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
that is promoted and the largest one that is not).

FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.

## Codebase areas involved (indicative)

- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.

## Acceptance criteria

AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.

AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.

AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.

AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.

## Assumptions

- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
  `%.1f` formatting.

## Out of scope

- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
- New dependencies.

## Constraints

- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
- `gofmt` formatting.

## Implementation plan
Plan format: 2
Plan status: DRAFT
Test level: std
Risk surfaces: shared-logic

### Decisions
**D1 — `IBytesN` keeps its current output.** `humanateBytes` also serves `IBytesN` (`bytes.go:150-153`), which the spec never names. FR1 lists five functions, FR5, FR6 and AC4 say five, and FR2 says every other output is unchanged, so `IBytesN` is not promoted, even though the Goal's wording («no byte formatter») would reach it. The requirements are the checkable text and this is the narrower reading: extending it later is one changed argument (`false` → `true`). The helper therefore gets an explicit parameter `promote bool`: `true` from `Bytes`, `BytesN`, `IBytes`; `false` from `IBytesN`. `humanateBytes` has no other caller (`bytes.go:115,128,138,152`) and no test calls it directly.

| input | output |
|---|---|
| `IBytesN(1_048_575, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
| `IBytesN(1_048_064, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
| `IBytesN(1_048_063, 2)` | `1023 KiB` (unchanged) |

**D2 — `humanateBytes`: promote after the rounding, without recursion.** Right after `val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding` and before the carry adjustment of `digits`:

```go
if promote && val >= base && int(e)+1 < len(sizes) {
	suffix = sizes[int(e)+1]
	val, intDigits = 1, 1
	digits = max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
}
```

These are the values `humanateBytes` computes for exactly one larger unit, so the string is the one FR1 requires for any `n` (`n` ≤ 1 gives no decimals). The comparison uses `base`, never a fixed 1000: `IBytes(1000 * 1024)` stays `1000 KiB`. `int(e)+1 < len(sizes)` is the FR3 guard: `Bytes` and `IBytes` cannot reach it (at most `18 EB` and `16 EiB`), it only protects the index.

**D3 — `humanateBigBytes`: same rule, with the rounding of `%.0f`.** Right after the `oomm` call, before `suffix := sizes[mag]`:

```go
if math.RoundToEven(val) >= float64(base.Int64()) && mag+1 < len(sizes) {
	val, mag = 1, mag+1
}
```

`%.0f` rounds half to even, as `math.RoundToEven` does: both 999.5 and 1023.5 reach the base. `val = 1` selects the existing `%.1f` format, hence `1.0 <unit>`. At the last unit `mag+1 == len(sizes)`: `1000 QB` and `1024 QiB` stay (FR3). `oomm` does not change, and the function still works on its copy `c`, so the `*big.Int` received is untouched (FR4).

**D4 — the boundaries are measured on the base, not derived.** Run on a copy of the base at commit 37bea5e. Above 2^53 `float64(s)` loses precision, so the two highest boundaries of `Bytes` and `IBytes` are not the exact half. 1	# Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
6	print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
7	that should have been written with the next unit:
8	
9	- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
10	- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
11	- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
12	- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.
13	
14	The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
15	(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
16	some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).
17	
18	## Goal
19	
20	No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
21	printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.
22	
23	## Functional requirements
24	
25	FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
26	print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
27	unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
28	larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
29	`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
30	`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.
31	
32	FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
33	current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
34	and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.
35	
36	FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
37	functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.
38	
39	FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.
40	
41	FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
42	test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
43	that is promoted and the largest one that is not).
44	
45	FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
46	shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.
47	
48	## Codebase areas involved (indicative)
49	
50	- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
51	- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
52	- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.
53	
54	## Acceptance criteria
55	
56	AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.
57	
58	AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
59	input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.
60	
61	AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.
62	
63	AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
64	back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.
65	
66	## Assumptions
67	
68	- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
69	  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
70	  `%.1f` formatting.
71	
72	## Out of scope
73	
74	- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
75	- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
76	- New dependencies.
77	
78	## Constraints
79	
80	- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
81	- `gofmt` formatting.
82

83	## Implementation plan
84	Plan format: 2
85	Plan status: DRAFT
86	Test level: std
87	Risk surfaces: shared-logic
88	
89	### Decisions
90	**D1 — `IBytesN` keeps its current output.** `humanateBytes` also serves `IBytesN` (`bytes.go:150-153`), which the spec never names. FR1 lists five functions, FR5, FR6 and AC4 say five, and FR2 says every other output is unchanged, so `IBytesN` is not promoted, even though the Goal's wording («no byte formatter») would reach it. The requirements are the checkable text and this is the narrower reading: extending it later is one changed argument (`false` → `true`). The helper therefore gets an explicit parameter `promote bool`: `true` from `Bytes`, `BytesN`, `IBytes`; `false` from `IBytesN`. `humanateBytes` has no other caller (`bytes.go:115,128,138,152`) and no test calls it directly.
91	
92	| input | output |
93	|---|---|
94	| `IBytesN(1_048_575, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
95	| `IBytesN(1_048_064, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
96	| `IBytesN(1_048_063, 2)` | `1023 KiB` (unchanged) |
97	
98	**D2 — `humanateBytes`: promote after the rounding, without recursion.** Right after `val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding` and before the carry adjustment of `digits`:
99	
100	```go
101	if promote && val >= base && int(e)+1 < len(sizes) {
102		suffix = sizes[int(e)+1]
103		val, intDigits = 1, 1
104		digits = max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
105	}
106	```
107	
108	These are the values `humanateBytes` computes for exactly one larger unit, so the string is the one FR1 requires for any `n` (`n` ≤ 1 gives no decimals). The comparison uses `base`, never a fixed 1000: `IBytes(1000 * 1024)` stays `1000 KiB`. `int(e)+1 < len(sizes)` is the FR3 guard: `Bytes` and `IBytes` cannot reach it (at most `18 EB` and `16 EiB`), it only protects the index.
109	
110	**D3 — `humanateBigBytes`: same rule, with the rounding of `%.0f`.** Right after the `oomm` call, before `suffix := sizes[mag]`:
111	
112	```go
113	if math.RoundToEven(val) >= float64(base.Int64()) && mag+1 < len(sizes) {
114		val, mag = 1, mag+1
115	}
116	```
117	
118	`%.0f` rounds half to even, as `math.RoundToEven` does: both 999.5 and 1023.5 reach the base. `val = 1` selects the existing `%.1f` format, hence `1.0 <unit>`. At the last unit `mag+1 == len(sizes)`: `1000 QB` and `1024 QiB` stay (FR3). `oomm` does not change, and the function still works on its copy `c`, so the `*big.Int` received is untouched (FR4).
119	
120	**D4 — the boundaries are measured on the base, not derived.** Run on a copy of the base at commit 37bea5e. Above 2^53 `float64(s)` loses precision, so the two highest boundaries of `Bytes` and `IBytes` are not the exact half. The «not promoted» column is the output today and stays; the «promoted» input prints `1000 <unit>` or `1024 <unit>` today.
121	
122	| function | largest not promoted | output | smallest promoted | output |
123	|---|---|---|---|---|
124	| `Bytes` | 999_499 | `999 kB` | 999_500 | `1.0 MB` |
125	| `Bytes` | 999_499_999 | `999 MB` | 999_500_000 | `1.0 GB` |
126	| `Bytes` | 999_499_999_999 | `999 GB` | 999_500_000_000 | `1.0 TB` |
127	| `Bytes` | 999_499_999_999_999 | `999 TB` | 999_500_000_000_000 | `1.0 PB` |
128	| `Bytes` | 999_499_999_999_999_935 | `999 PB` | 999_499_999_999_999_936 | `1.0 EB` |
129	| `IBytes` | 1_048_063 | `1023 KiB` | 1_048_064 | `1.0 MiB` |
130	| `IBytes` | 1_073_217_535 | `1023 MiB` | 1_073_217_536 | `1.0 GiB` |
131	| `IBytes` | 1_098_974_756_863 | `1023 GiB` | 1_098_974_756_864 | `1.0 TiB` |
132	| `IBytes` | 1_125_350_151_028_735 | `1023 TiB` | 1_125_350_151_028_736 | `1.0 PiB` |
133	| `IBytes` | 1_152_358_554_653_425_599 | `1023 PiB` | 1_152_358_554_653_425_600 | `1.0 EiB` |
134	
135	`BigBytes`, for each unit `U` from `kB` to `RB`: 999.5 `U` is the smallest promoted (`1.0` next unit) and 999.5 `U` − 1 the largest not promoted (`999 U`). `BigIBytes`, from `KiB` to `RiB`: 1023.5 `U` and 1023.5 `U` − 1 (`1023 U`). `BytesN` depends on `n`:
136	
137	| `n` | largest not promoted | output | smallest promoted | output |
138	|---|---|---|---|---|
139	| -1, 0, 1 | 999_499 | `999 kB` | 999_500 | `1 MB` |
140	| 2 | 999_499 | `999 kB` | 999_500 | `1.0 MB` |
141	| 3 | 999_499 | `999 kB` | 999_500 | `1.00 MB` |
142	| 4 | 999_949 | `999.9 kB` | 999_950 | `1.000 MB` |
143	| 5 | 999_994 | `999.99 kB` | 999_995 | `1.0000 MB` |
144	| 7 | 999_999 | `999.9990 kB` | none in that unit | — |
145	
146	Other unchanged outputs and FR3:
147	
148	| input | output |
149	|---|---|
150	| `Bytes(9)`, `IBytes(9)`, `BytesN(9, 3)` | `9 B` |
151	| `Bytes(999)` / `IBytes(1023)` | `999 B` / `1023 B` |
152	| `IBytes(1000 * 1024)` / `IBytes(1023 * 1024)` | `1000 KiB` / `1023 KiB` |
153	| `Bytes(math.MaxUint64)` / `IBytes(math.MaxUint64)` | `18 EB` / `16 EiB` |
154	| `BigBytes` of 1000 QB − 1, of 1000 QB, of 5000 QB | `1000 QB`, `1000 QB`, `5000 QB` |
155	| `BigIBytes` of 1024 QiB − 1, of 1024 QiB | `1024 QiB`, `1024 QiB` |
156	
157	**D5 — a position in the test file.** `testList.validate` reports its errors from `common_test.go`, so a failing row of `TestBytes` carries no position in the test that declares it, and the test-red phase needs that position. `common_test.go` is outside the write scope of that phase (it holds no row of the test table), so it stays untouched: `bytes_test.go` gets the helper `func (tl testList) validateHere(t *testing.T)`, with `t.Helper()` as first line and the same comparison and the same message as `validate`. `TestBytes`, `TestBigBytes` and T3 to T7 call it; every other test keeps `validate`. No change to what any test asserts.
158	
159	**D6 — the parse-back of AC4.** Each promoted case of T3 to T7 also parses its output back (`ParseBytes` or `ParseBigBytes`) and requires exactly one larger unit. Non-promoted outputs do not change and neither does the parser.
160	
161	Other implications: API, data, persistence, permissions, UI, migration: no implication (AC4: exported names and signatures unchanged; both helpers are unexported). Rollback: revert the working-tree changes, nothing is persisted. Docs (FR6): no wrong example exists: the doc comments of `bytes.go` and `bigbytes.go` and `README.markdown:22` show 83 MB, 82.9 MB, 82.85 MB, 79 MiB; searched for `1000 ` and `1024 ` in `README.markdown`, only the `Comma` example at line 63 matches.
162	
163	### Touched files
164	- `bytes.go`
165	- `bigbytes.go`
166	- `bytes_test.go`
167	- `bigbytes_test.go`
168	
169	### Steps

1	# Spec: byte sizes that round up to 1000 (or 1024) must move to the next unit
2	
3	## Context
4	
5	The byte-size formatters of this Go module choose the unit from the exact value and then round the number they
6	print. Close below a unit boundary the rounding carries the number up to the base, and the output shows a number
7	that should have been written with the next unit:
8	
9	- `Bytes(999_999)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.0 MB"`;
10	- `IBytes(1_048_575)` (1 MiB − 1) returns `"1024 KiB"` instead of `"1.0 MiB"`;
11	- `BigBytes(big.NewInt(999_999))` returns `"1000 kB"`, `BigIBytes` of 1 MiB − 1 returns `"1024 KiB"`;
12	- `BytesN(999_999, 3)` returns `"1000 kB"` instead of `"1.00 MB"`.
13	
14	The formatters are in `bytes.go` (`Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`, helper `humanateBytes`) and `bigbytes.go`
15	(`BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`, helper `humanateBigBytes`). Tests are next to them (`bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`);
16	some existing test cases currently expect the wrong outputs above (for example `"1000 kB"` for `MByte - Byte`).
17	
18	## Goal
19	
20	No byte formatter prints a number equal to or larger than its base when a larger unit exists; such values are
21	printed exactly as the value of one unit of the next size is printed.
22	
23	## Functional requirements
24	
25	FR1. For `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN` (any `n`), `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes`: when the number that the function would
26	print, after its own rounding, is greater than or equal to the base (1000 for SI, 1024 for IEC) and the function's
27	unit list has a larger unit, the result is the string that the same function returns for exactly one of that
28	larger unit. Examples: `Bytes(999_999) == Bytes(1_000_000) == "1.0 MB"`; `Bytes(999_500) == "1.0 MB"`;
29	`IBytes(1_048_575) == "1.0 MiB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 3) == "1.00 MB"`; `BytesN(999_999, 0) == BytesN(1_000_000, 0)`;
30	`BigBytes` of 10⁹ − 1 `== "1.0 GB"`; `BigIBytes` of 1 GiB − 1 `== "1.0 GiB"`.
31	
32	FR2. Every other output is unchanged. In particular values whose rounded number stays below the base keep their
33	current output: `Bytes(999_499) == "999 kB"`, `IBytes(1000 * 1024) == "1000 KiB"`, `IBytes(1023 * 1024) == "1023 KiB"`,
34	and all outputs for values below 10 bytes.
35	
36	FR3. There is no unit after the last one: for the largest unit of a function (`QB` and `QiB` for the `Big`
37	functions) the number is printed as today, even when it is 1000 (or 1024) or more.
38	
39	FR4. `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` still do not modify the `*big.Int` they receive.
40	
41	FR5. The existing test cases that encode the wrong outputs of the Context are corrected to the new outputs, and new
42	test cases cover FR1 to FR4 for each of the five functions, including the exact boundary values (the smallest input
43	that is promoted and the largest one that is not).
44	
45	FR6. The doc comments of the five functions stay correct; if an example in a doc comment or in `README.markdown`
46	shows one of the wrong outputs, it is corrected.
47	
48	## Codebase areas involved (indicative)
49	
50	- `bytes.go`: `humanateBytes`, `Bytes`, `IBytes`, `BytesN`.
51	- `bigbytes.go`: `humanateBigBytes`, `oomm`, `BigBytes`, `BigIBytes`.
52	- `bytes_test.go`, `bigbytes_test.go`.
53	
54	## Acceptance criteria
55	
56	AC1. Every example in FR1, FR2 and FR3 holds.
57	
58	AC2. For every SI and IEC unit boundary reachable by each function, the smallest promoted input and the largest
59	input that is not promoted give the outputs required by FR1 and FR2.
60	
61	AC3. `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` pass; `gofmt -l .` prints nothing.
62	
63	AC4. The public API (exported names and signatures) is unchanged, and `ParseBytes` / `ParseBigBytes` still read
64	back every output of the five formatters to a value within one unit of the last printed digit.
65	
66	## Assumptions
67	
68	- "The number the function would print" is the number after the rounding each function already does: `Bytes`,
69	  `IBytes` and `BytesN` round half up to their number of digits, `BigBytes` and `BigIBytes` use Go's `%.0f` /
70	  `%.1f` formatting.
71	
72	## Out of scope
73	
74	- Any other change to formatting (number of digits, spacing, unit names) or to parsing.
75	- The other formatters of the module (`Comma`, `SI`, `Ftoa`, times, ordinals).
76	- New dependencies.
77	
78	## Constraints
79	
80	- The Go version declared in `go.mod`; standard library only.
81	- `gofmt` formatting.

89	### Decisions
90	**D1 — `IBytesN` keeps its current output.** `humanateBytes` also serves `IBytesN` (`bytes.go:150-153`), which the spec never names. FR1 lists five functions, FR5, FR6 and AC4 say five, and FR2 says every other output is unchanged, so `IBytesN` is not promoted, even though the Goal's wording («no byte formatter») would reach it. The requirements are the checkable text and this is the narrower reading: extending it later is one changed argument (`false` → `true`). The helper therefore gets an explicit parameter `promote bool`: `true` from `Bytes`, `BytesN`, `IBytes`; `false` from `IBytesN`. `humanateBytes` has no other caller (`bytes.go:115,128,138,152`) and no test calls it directly.
91	
92	| input | output |
93	|---|---|
94	| `IBytesN(1_048_575, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
95	| `IBytesN(1_048_064, 2)` | `1024 KiB` (unchanged) |
96	| `IBytesN(1_048_063, 2)` | `1023 KiB` (unchanged) |
97	
98	**D2 — `humanateBytes`: promote after the rounding, without recursion.** Right after `val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding` and before the carry adjustment of `digits`:
99	
100	```go
101	if promote && val >= base && int(e)+1 < len(sizes) {
102		suffix = sizes[int(e)+1]
103		val, intDigits = 1, 1
104		digits = max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
105	}
106	```
107	
108	These are the values `humanateBytes` computes for exactly one larger unit, so the string is the one FR1 requires for any `n` (`n` ≤ 1 gives no decimals). The comparison uses `base`, never a fixed 1000: `IBytes(1000 * 1024)` stays `1000 KiB`. `int(e)+1 < len(sizes)` is the FR3 guard: `Bytes` and `IBytes` cannot reach it (at most `18 EB` and `16 EiB`), it only protects the index.
109	
110	**D3 — `humanateBigBytes`: same rule, with the rounding of `%.0f`.** Right after the `oomm` call, before `suffix := sizes[mag]`:
111	
112	```go
113	if math.RoundToEven(val) >= float64(base.Int64()) && mag+1 < len(sizes) {
114		val, mag = 1, mag+1
115	}
116	```
117	
118	`%.0f` rounds half to even, as `math.RoundToEven` does: both 999.5 and 1023.5 reach the base. `val = 1` selects the existing `%.1f` format, hence `1.0 <unit>`. At the last unit `mag+1 == len(sizes)`: `1000 QB` and `1024 QiB` stay (FR3). `oomm` does not change, and the function still works on its copy `c`, so the `*big.Int` received is untouched (FR4).

120	**D4 — the boundaries are measured on the base, not derived.** Run on a copy of the base at commit 37bea5e. Above 2^53 `float64(s)` loses precision, so the two highest boundaries of `Bytes` and `IBytes` are not the exact half. The «not promoted» column is the output today and stays; the «promoted» input prints `1000 <unit>` or `1024 <unit>` today.

65	func logn(n, b float64) float64 {
66		return math.Log(n) / math.Log(b)
67	}
68	
69	func countDigits(n int64) int {
70		digits := 0
71		for n != 0 {
72			n /= 10
73			digits += 1
74		}
75		return digits
76	}
77	
78	func humanateBytes(s uint64, base float64, minDigits int, sizes []string) string {
79		if s < 10 {
80			return fmt.Sprintf("%d B", s)
81		}
82		e := math.Floor(logn(float64(s), base))
83		suffix := sizes[int(e)]
84		val := float64(s) / math.Pow(base, e)
85	
86		// Determine how many decimal places to keep based on the unrounded
87		// value's integer-digit count, then round exactly once to that
88		// precision. Rounding first to a fixed precision and then again when
89		// formatting (double rounding) can flip the result at a boundary due
90		// to floating point error (see #103).
91		intDigits := countDigits(int64(val))
92		digits := max(minDigits-intDigits, 0)
93		rounding := math.Pow10(digits)
94		val = math.Floor(val*rounding+0.5) / rounding
95	
96		// Rounding may have carried into an additional integer digit (e.g.
97		// 9.996 -> 10.0), which means fewer decimal places should be shown
98		// than originally computed.
99		if newIntDigits := countDigits(int64(val)); newIntDigits > intDigits {
100			digits = max(digits-(newIntDigits-intDigits), 0)
101		}
102	
103		ff := "%%.%df %%s"
104		f := fmt.Sprintf(ff, digits)
105		return fmt.Sprintf(f, val, suffix)
106	}

114		sizes := []string{"B", "kB", "MB", "GB", "TB", "PB", "EB"}
115		return humanateBytes(s, 1000, 2, sizes)
116	}

155	// ParseBytes parses a string representation of bytes into the number
156	// of bytes it represents.
157	//
158	// See Also: Bytes, IBytes.
159	//
160	// ParseBytes("42 MB") -> 42000000, nil
161	// ParseBytes("42 mib") -> 44040192, nil
162	func ParseBytes(s string) (uint64, error) {
163		lastDigit := 0
164		hasComma := false
165		for _, r := range s {
166			if !(unicode.IsDigit(r) || r == '.' || r == ',') {
167				break
168			}
169			if r == ',' {
170				hasComma = true
171			}
172			lastDigit++
173		}
174	
175		num := s[:lastDigit]
176		if hasComma {
177			num = strings.Replace(num, ",", "", -1)
178		}
179	
180		f, err := strconv.ParseFloat(num, 64)
181		if err != nil {
182			return 0, err
183		}
184	
185		extra := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(s[lastDigit:]))
186		if m, ok := bytesSizeTable[extra]; ok {
187			// Parse whole-number inputs exactly. A float64 cannot represent
188			// integers above 2^53, and the multiplication below would also reject
189			// otherwise-valid values near math.MaxUint64, so route integers through
190			// uint64 arithmetic with an overflow check.
191			if !strings.ContainsRune(num, '.') {
192				if v, perr := strconv.ParseUint(num, 10, 64); perr == nil {
193					if hi, lo := bits.Mul64(v, m); hi == 0 {
194						return lo, nil
195					}
196					return 0, fmt.Errorf("too large: %v", s)
197				}
198			}
199			f *= float64(m)
200			if f >= math.MaxUint64 {
201				return 0, fmt.Errorf("too large: %v", s)
202			}
203			return uint64(f), nil
204		}
205	
206		return 0, fmt.Errorf("unhandled size name: %v", extra)
207	}
